title: The Five Demons You Must Slay To Implement Change
author: MutuallyAssuredInstruction
summary: MutuallyAssuredInstruction identifies five recurring failure modes — demons — that reliably destroy educational change initiatives before they take hold. The article is addressed to school leaders and instructional coaches who have experienced the frustration of a well-designed change effort that simply did not survive contact with the organization. The five demons are: the illusion of consensus (people nod without genuine buy-in), the seduction of novelty (change is treated as an end rather than a means), the complexity trap (implementation becomes too elaborate to survive real conditions), the feedback desert (no mechanism exists for knowing whether change is working), and the sustainability problem (change depends on one person's energy rather than structural embedding). Each demon receives a concrete diagnostic and a specific countermeasure. The piece argues that successful change is not an ideas problem but an organizational problem — and that leaders who treat it as such build the conditions for change to survive beyond its initial excitement.
points: The illusion of consensus is the most dangerous demon: when leaders mistake polite meeting agreement for genuine buy-in, they proceed without the real commitment needed to sustain effort through the difficult middle of a change process.

Novelty addiction derails change by treating the launch of an initiative as an achievement in itself — schools that celebrate launching consistently abandon initiatives before they produce results because the excitement has faded and the hard work of embedding has not been done.

The complexity trap kills otherwise viable initiatives: the more elaborate the rollout, the more failure points exist, and organizations under pressure default to familiar routines the moment the new system breaks down.

The feedback desert means leaders cannot distinguish between implementation that is actually working and implementation that is merely occurring; building early feedback loops before full deployment is essential to catching failure while it can still be corrected.

The sustainability problem is a design flaw: any change that requires a specific leader's personal energy to maintain is one personnel change away from extinction — embedding change in structures and routines rather than in individuals is the only durable strategy.
